title: Quantum Field Theory
subject: Particles & Fields
summary: A first, calculation-oriented introduction to relativistic quantum field theory: fields as oscillators, canonical quantization, propagators and Feynman diagrams, the Dirac equation, tree-level QED, a conceptual treatment of renormalization and the renormalization group, and gauge symmetry and the Higgs mechanism.

units.title: From oscillators to fields
units.summary: Why relativity plus quantum mechanics forces a field description; Lagrangian field theory and Noether's theorem; second quantization (the Fock-space formalism also used in quantum chemistry).

lessons.title: Why quantum field theory?
objectives: Explain why single-particle relativistic quantum mechanics fails: Klein-Gordon negative probability densities and negative energies, and pair creation at energies around mc^2.
State the argument that combining locality, special relativity, and quantum mechanics leads naturally to fields with variable particle number and antiparticles.
Work in natural units (hbar = c = 1) and convert mass, length, time, energy, and cross-section between natural and SI units.
Compute a Compton wavelength and use it to say when a process needs QFT (for instance, photons as quantized electromagnetic oscillators; phonons in a crystal as the same idea).

readings.title: A first stab at relativistic quantum mechanics

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Why Quantum Field Theory

demoIdeas: Pair-creation threshold explorer: photon energy versus electron-positron production, with Compton wavelength vs. confinement length.

lessons.title: Classical field theory and the Lagrangian density
objectives: Derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for a field from the principle of least action.
Write the Lagrangian density for a real scalar field and derive the Klein-Gordon equation from it.
Write the Maxwell Lagrangian -(1/4) F^2 and recover Maxwell's equations from it.
Compute the canonical momentum pi = partial L / partial (partial_t phi) and the Hamiltonian density.
Take the continuum limit of a chain of coupled oscillators to obtain the wave equation (the origin of 'fields as oscillators').

readings.title: Examples of Lagrangians, or how to write down a theory

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Classical Field Theories and Principle of Locality

demoIdeas: Chain of coupled masses and springs whose normal modes approach a continuous string as N grows.

lessons.title: Symmetries, Noether's theorem, and conserved currents
objectives: State and derive Noether's theorem for a continuous symmetry of a field theory, giving a conserved current j^mu with partial_mu j^mu = 0.
Derive the energy-momentum tensor T^{mu nu} from spacetime translation invariance and compute the Hamiltonian and momentum of a scalar field.
Find the conserved U(1) charge of a complex scalar field.
Explain how the Lorentz group acts on fields and which conserved quantities Lorentz invariance gives (angular momentum and boosts).

lectures.title: Lecture 2: Symmetries and Conservation Laws

demoIdeas: Complex scalar field on a 1D lattice with a U(1) phase rotation: visualize the conserved charge density flowing as a current.

lessons.title: Second quantization and Fock space
objectives: Quantize the harmonic oscillator with ladder operators a and a-dagger, [a, a-dagger] = 1, and build number eigenstates.
Construct the Fock space of many identical bosons from occupation numbers and show how creation and annihilation operators change particle number.
Write one-body operators in second-quantized form sum_ij t_ij a_i-dagger a_j and explain how this is the language of quantum-chemistry electronic Hamiltonians (fermionic version anticipated).
Show that a chain of coupled oscillators has normal modes whose quanta are phonons.
demoIdeas: Fock-space explorer: apply a and a-dagger to superpositions of number states and watch occupation probabilities change.

units.title: The free scalar field
units.summary: Canonical quantization of the Klein-Gordon field: particles as excitations, antiparticles, causality, the Feynman propagator, and force from particle exchange (Yukawa).

lessons.title: Canonical quantization of the real scalar field
objectives: Expand the Klein-Gordon field in Fourier modes and identify each mode as a harmonic oscillator with frequency omega_p = sqrt(p^2 + m^2).
Impose the equal-time commutator [phi(x), pi(y)] = i delta^3(x - y) and derive [a_p, a_q-dagger] = (2 pi)^3 delta^3(p - q).
Write H as an integral of omega_p a-dagger a plus a divergent zero-point energy and remove the latter by normal ordering.
Construct one-particle states |p> = a_p-dagger |0>, compute their energy and momentum, and use relativistic normalization.

demoIdeas: Mode-sum visualizer: build a localized wave packet from a_p-dagger superpositions and watch it propagate.

lessons.title: The complex scalar field, antiparticles, and charge
objectives: Quantize a complex scalar field with two sets of operators and identify particles and antiparticles with opposite charge.
Compute the conserved charge Q = integral of (a-dagger a - b-dagger b) and the eigenvalues on one-particle states.
Show how time dependence follows in the Heisenberg picture and compute the Lorentz-invariant measure d^3p / (2 E_p).
Explain why relativity and causality require antiparticles, and cite positron emission tomography (annihilation into 511 keV photons) as a chemical application.

lessons.title: Causality and the Feynman propagator
objectives: Compute the commutator [phi(x), phi(y)] and show it vanishes for spacelike separations.

Define the Feynman propagator as the time-ordered vacuum correlator and derive its momentum-space form i/(p^2 - m^2 + i epsilon) by contour integration, explaining the role of the i epsilon prescription (complex analysis from M6).
Interpret the propagator as a Green's function of the Klein-Gordon operator.
Distinguish on-shell from off-shell (virtual) momenta.

lessons.title: Forces from particle exchange: the Yukawa potential
objectives: Show that a static source coupled to a massive scalar field produces the Yukawa potential V(r) = -g^2 e^{-mr} / (4 pi r).
Relate the range of the force to the exchanged particle's mass, 1/m, and estimate the pion-exchange range (about 1.4 fm).
Contrast scalar exchange (attractive between like sources) with photon exchange (m = 0, Coulomb).
Recognize the screened Coulomb potential of Debye-Huckel theory in electrolytes and Thomas-Fermi screening in metals as the same mathematical form.
demoIdeas: Yukawa versus Coulomb potential plot with a mass slider and a toy Debye-length slider for an electrolyte.

units.title: Interacting fields and Feynman diagrams
units.summary: The S-matrix, Dyson series, Wick's theorem, Feynman rules in position and momentum space, and cross sections: the working machinery of perturbative QFT.

lessons.title: The interaction picture and the S-matrix
objectives: Derive the interaction picture and the Dyson series U = T exp(-i integral of H_I dt).
Define the S-matrix and relate its elements to the invariant amplitude A through (2 pi)^4 delta^4(sum p).
Write interaction Hamiltonians for phi^4 and Yukawa theories and identify their couplings and mass dimensions.
Explain asymptotic in and out states and the idea of LSZ reduction.

lessons.title: Wick's theorem and contractions
objectives: State Wick's theorem relating time-ordered products to normal-ordered products plus contractions.
Compute a four-point time-ordered correlator in free scalar theory by listing contractions.
Map the contractions in the second-order nucleon-nucleon scattering amplitude in Yukawa theory onto diagrams.
Explain why normal ordering removes tadpoles and vacuum bubbles cancel in the S-matrix.

lessons.title: Feynman rules in momentum space
objectives: State the Feynman rules for phi^4 and Yukawa theories: vertices, propagators, momentum conservation, loop integrals.
Draw all diagrams at a given order and assign symmetry factors.
Distinguish connected from disconnected, and tree from loop, diagrams.
Compute the tree-level 2 -> 2 amplitude in phi^4 (A = -lambda) and identify the s, t, and u channels with Mandelstam variables.

lessons.title: Cross sections and decay rates
objectives: Define decay rates and cross sections from |A|^2 and relativistic phase space.
Derive the center-of-mass differential cross section dsigma/dOmega = |A|^2 p_f / (64 pi^2 s p_i).
Compute the decay rate of a heavy scalar into two lighter scalars.
Connect to the Fermi golden rule from P6 and to unitarity (optical theorem, stated).
Relate cross section to the measurable scattering rate in an experiment such as X-ray or neutron scattering.

units.title: The Dirac equation and fermion fields
units.summary: Spin-1/2 particles: the Dirac equation, gamma matrices, spinor solutions and antiparticles, quantization with anticommutators, and discrete symmetries.

lessons.title: The Dirac equation and gamma matrices
objectives: Derive the Dirac equation by demanding a first-order equation whose square is the Klein-Gordon equation.
Use the Clifford algebra {gamma^mu, gamma^nu} = 2 eta^{mu nu} and build the Weyl (chiral) representation.
Show how spinors transform under Lorentz transformations and why psi-bar psi is a scalar and psi-bar gamma^mu psi a vector.
Write the Dirac Lagrangian and relate it to relativistic effects in chemistry: spin-orbit coupling and the g = 2 electron, which make gold yellow and mercury liquid.

lessons.title: Dirac solutions, chirality, and antiparticles
objectives: Solve the Dirac equation for plane waves, u(p) and v(p), and compute spin sums sum u u-bar = pslash + m.
Define helicity and chirality (gamma^5) and write left- and right-handed Weyl spinors; analyze the massless limit.
Interpret negative-energy solutions as antiparticles (hole picture) and explain why this resolves the instability.
Take the nonrelativistic limit to get the Pauli equation with g = 2.

lessons.title: Quantizing the Dirac field
objectives: Expand the Dirac field in creation and annihilation operators and impose anticommutation relations.
Show that commutators would give an unbounded-below Hamiltonian, so anticommutators (Fermi statistics) are required.
Derive the Dirac propagator S_F = i(pslash + m)/(p^2 - m^2 + i epsilon).
Connect the anticommutation rules to the Pauli exclusion principle and Slater determinants in electronic-structure theory.

lessons.title: Discrete symmetries and fermion bilinears
objectives: Define the actions of C, P, and T on scalar and Dirac fields.
Classify the fermion bilinears (scalar, pseudoscalar, vector, axial vector, tensor) by their Lorentz and parity transformation.
State the CPT theorem and note the violation of parity (and C) in weak interactions as the link to S1.

units.title: Quantum electrodynamics
units.summary: Quantizing the photon, local U(1) gauge invariance, QED Feynman rules, and tree-level processes: Compton scattering, e+e- annihilation, and Coulomb scattering.

lessons.title: Quantizing the electromagnetic field
objectives: Explain gauge redundancy of A_mu and the need to fix a gauge (Lorenz or Coulomb gauge).
Quantize the photon field in Coulomb gauge and count its two physical polarizations.
State the photon propagator in Feynman gauge -i eta_{mu nu}/(k^2 + i epsilon) and the polarization sum.
Relate the quantized radiation field to spontaneous emission and the selection rules used in spectroscopy.

lessons.title: The QED Lagrangian and Feynman rules
objectives: Obtain the QED Lagrangian by minimal coupling D_mu = partial_mu + i e A_mu and show that local U(1) invariance fixes the interaction.
State the QED Feynman rules (vertex -i e gamma^mu, fermion and photon propagators, external spinors and polarizations).
Draw all lowest-order diagrams for a given process.
Explain the Ward identity and why gauge-dependent terms drop out of physical amplitudes.

lessons.title: Compton scattering at tree level
objectives: Use trace identities for gamma matrices to compute spin-summed |A|^2.
Compute the tree-level amplitude for electron-photon scattering and obtain the Klein-Nishina cross section.
Recover the Thomson cross section sigma_T = 8 pi alpha^2 / (3 m^2) in the low-energy limit and the Compton shift Delta lambda = (h/mc)(1 - cos theta).
Relate the result to X-ray scattering and Thomson scattering used in chemical crystallography.

lessons.title: Electron-positron annihilation, Coulomb scattering, and crossing
objectives: Compute the cross section for e+ e- -> mu+ mu- at high energy and the angular distribution (1 + cos^2 theta).
Use crossing symmetry to relate different QED processes (e.g., Bhabha and Moller scattering) to a single amplitude.
Compute Coulomb (Mott) scattering of an electron off a static nucleus from t-channel photon exchange.
State the R-ratio and its relation to the number of quark colors (link to S1).

units.title: Renormalization (conceptual)
units.summary: What divergences mean physically: power counting, regularization, charge renormalization and the running coupling, the renormalization group, and effective field theory (connecting to critical phenomena in P7).

lessons.title: Loop integrals, divergences, and regularization
objectives: Compute the superficial degree of divergence of a diagram by power counting and classify theories as renormalizable or not by the mass dimension of their couplings.
Evaluate a one-loop integral with a momentum cutoff and show a logarithmic divergence, then use Feynman parameters and Wick rotation to evaluate it in dimensional regularization.
Identify the divergent one-loop diagrams of QED: electron self-energy, vertex correction, and vacuum polarization.
Explain the physical idea of quasiparticle 'dressing' (compare the effective mass of an electron in a solid).

readings.title: Renormalization: the problem and its solution
Renormalization, quasiparticles and the Fermi surface

lectures.source: MIT OCW 8.323 Relativistic Quantum Field Theory I (Liu, Spring 2023)
lectures.title: Lecture 26: Quantum Fluctuations and Renormalization

lessons.title: Renormalizing QED and the running coupling
objectives: Explain charge renormalization through vacuum polarization: bare versus physical charge and the role of counterterms.
State the one-loop running coupling alpha(Q^2) and its measured value near 1/128 at the Z mass.
Describe the Lamb shift and the electron anomalous magnetic moment a_e = alpha/(2 pi) (Schwinger) as precision tests.
Interpret vacuum polarization as screening by virtual pairs, analogous to dielectric polarization in matter (Griffiths EM, P5).

readings.title: Renormalization in action: propagators and Feynman diagrams
The renormalization of QED and two great results

lessons.title: The renormalization group and effective field theory
objectives: Compute the one-loop beta function of phi^4 theory and interpret the sign of the running.
Explain Wilson's picture: integrating out high-momentum modes, relevant versus irrelevant operators, and fixed points.
Connect the renormalization group to critical phenomena and universality in the Ising model (P7).
Explain why low-energy physics is insensitive to short-distance details, with examples (Fermi theory of the weak interaction; effective Hamiltonians and pseudopotentials in chemistry).
demoIdeas: Block-spin RG flow for the 2D Ising model, showing flow to the ordered, disordered, or critical fixed point.

units.title: Gauge symmetry and the Higgs mechanism (conceptual)
units.summary: Spontaneous symmetry breaking, non-abelian gauge theory and QCD, and the Higgs mechanism of the electroweak theory, linking to S1.

lessons.title: Spontaneous symmetry breaking and Goldstone bosons
objectives: Analyze a scalar potential with negative mass squared (Mexican hat), find the vacuum manifold, and expand around a chosen vacuum.
State and illustrate Goldstone's theorem: one massless boson per broken continuous global symmetry generator.
Give examples: ferromagnet (magnons), chiral symmetry breaking in QCD (pions), and superfluid phonons.
Connect the order parameter and Landau free energy of P7 to the field-theory potential.
demoIdeas: Mexican-hat potential in 3D with a ball in the potential showing radial (massive) and angular (massless Goldstone) oscillations.

lessons.title: Non-abelian gauge theory and QCD
objectives: Construct an SU(N) gauge theory: covariant derivative, field strength with its self-interaction term.
State the QCD beta function and explain asymptotic freedom and confinement qualitatively.
Compute simple color factors and relate quarks and gluons to the particle spectrum of S1.

lessons.title: The Higgs mechanism and the electroweak theory
objectives: Show in the abelian Higgs model how the gauge boson acquires mass while the Goldstone boson is eaten, and count degrees of freedom.
Describe the SU(2) x U(1) electroweak theory: W and Z masses, the weak mixing angle, and how the photon stays massless.
Explain the discovery of the Higgs boson (about 125 GeV) and how fermion masses arise from Yukawa couplings.
Use the Meissner effect in superconductors as an analogy for giving the photon an effective mass.
